summary: This RFC extends SIP with a framework for nodes to subscribe to and receive notifications about events from other nodes. It is deliberately not a general-purpose infrastructure for all kinds of event subscriptions.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6665 lets a SIP user agent request updates when a resource changes, such as presence or mailbox state. The notifier sends current state and later changes using NOTIFY requests, while an event package defines exactly what the updates mean.

questions: how does sip subscribe and notify work
what is sip subscribe and notify
how do i poll sip resource state
subtitle: A SIP framework for subscribing to state changes and receiving notifications.

tldr.problem: SIP services need to tell one node when state changes at another node, without requiring the subscriber to ask repeatedly.
tldr.mechanism: A subscriber sends SUBSCRIBE for an event package. The notifier responds and sends an immediate NOTIFY with current state, then sends further NOTIFY requests as state changes until the subscription ends.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6665 provides a framework that event packages must extend; it is not a standalone notification service. It obsoletes RFC 3265 and is updated by RFC 7621.

today: RFC 6665 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3265 and updates RFC 3261 and RFC 4660. It has been updated by RFC 7621.

sections.title: Why SIP Uses Event Notifications
sections.content:
SIP services such as automatic callback, buddy lists, message-waiting indications and call-status reporting can need state from another node. Repeated requests for updates can be replaced by a subscription that notifies a user agent when state changes.

RFC 6665 defines the framework for SIP event notification. It is deliberately not a general-purpose notification system, and it cannot be used alone: another specification, called an event package, must define the event and the state information reported.

The framework uses SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY and revises the earlier mechanism in RFC 3265 based on implementation experience.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP user agent can subscribe to state changes instead of repeatedly asking for the latest state. An event package must define what kind of state the subscription covers.

sections.title: Subscribers, Notifiers and Event Packages
sections.content:
A subscriber receives NOTIFY requests about a resource and typically sends the SUBSCRIBE requests that create subscriptions. A notifier generates those NOTIFY requests and typically accepts SUBSCRIBE requests.

A subscription is application state associated with a SIP dialog. It includes the dialog, the event package name and possibly an identification token. An event package defines what state a notifier reports and the syntax and meaning of that information.

A notifier acts as a user agent when it accepts subscriptions and sends notifications, even if the node also performs another SIP role such as proxying.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscriber asks to receive updates, and the notifier sends them. The event package defines what the updates describe.

sections.title: SUBSCRIBE, NOTIFY and Their Headers
sections.content:
SUBSCRIBE requests current state and later updates. It should include an Expires header stating the requested duration. A successful response must include Expires and may shorten, but must not lengthen, the requested duration. Expires set to zero requests an unsubscribe and also fetches current state.

Each SUBSCRIBE must contain exactly one Event header naming the event package. An optional Accept header lists the body types the subscriber can receive. The notifier's NOTIFY must use the same Event value and carries state in its body or a URI pointing to that state.

Every NOTIFY must include Subscription-State, with a value of active, pending or terminated. A single NOTIFY does not end an active subscription. The RFC also defines Allow-Events and response code 489 (Bad Event).
sections.plainLanguage: SUBSCRIBE names the event and how long updates are wanted. NOTIFY carries the state and says whether the subscription is active, waiting for approval or finished.

sections.title: The Subscription Lifecycle
sections.content:
A subscriber moves from init to notify_wait after sending SUBSCRIBE. A NOTIFY reporting pending or active creates a subscription. Pending means the notifier has received the request but does not yet have enough policy information to approve or reject it.

The subscriber starts Timer N when it sends SUBSCRIBE; Timer N is 64*T1. If no NOTIFY arrives before the timer expires, the attempt is considered failed. A terminated NOTIFY, certain refresh failures or a timeout can end a subscription. Forking may create several independent subscriptions from one SUBSCRIBE, each with its own state and timers.

A terminating NOTIFY may include a reason such as deactivated, probation, rejected, timeout, giveup, noresource or invariant. The reason and optional retry-after value guide whether the subscriber should try again.
sections.plainLanguage: After sending SUBSCRIBE, the subscriber waits for a NOTIFY that establishes the subscription. A subscription later ends through a terminating NOTIFY, an unsuccessful refresh or a timer expiring.

sections.title: Creating, Refreshing and Polling
sections.content:
When a notifier accepts or refreshes a subscription, it must send a NOTIFY immediately with current state, even if authorization is still pending. The notifier must answer SUBSCRIBE without waiting for a human decision. It may use 423 (Interval Too Brief) and Min-Expires when a requested duration is too short.

The subscriber refreshes the subscription by sending another SUBSCRIBE on the same dialog before it expires. If a refresh receives specified errors such as 404, 410, 489 or 604, the subscriber treats the subscription as terminated. A notifier that removes an expired subscription should send a terminating NOTIFY with reason timeout.

A SUBSCRIBE with Expires zero can fetch state without keeping a subscription. The RFC calls this polling and advises using it sparingly, especially when it would create more messages than a long-running subscription. SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY transactions cannot be canceled.
sections.plainLanguage: The notifier sends the current state as soon as it accepts a subscription, then sends updates when state changes. A subscriber must refresh before expiry; it can use Expires zero for a one-time fetch, but frequent polling adds network traffic.

sections.title: What Event Packages Must Define
sections.content:
An event package must define the event name, the request and notification body types, notifier and subscriber behavior, handling of forked requests, and the maximum notification rate. Package authors should confirm that SIP is suitable; the RFC cautions against very frequent events, such as more than about once per second.

Packages should report complete, well-defined state rather than only a stream of events. For relatively small state, the RFC suggests sending the full state with each notification. For large state, a package may define deltas: the first notification contains full state, later notifications contain changes, and a version number increases by exactly one each time.

If a subscriber detects a gap in delta versions, it ignores the incomplete change and sends SUBSCRIBE again to request a full state snapshot. A package cannot weaken requirements marked MUST or SHOULD in the framework.
sections.plainLanguage: An event package defines the name, message format, update rules and notification rate for one kind of state. If it sends only changes, it must provide a way to detect missing changes and request a full state again.

sections.title: Access Control and Privacy
sections.content:
Resource state can be private, so the notifier's user should control who may subscribe. Notifiers should use SIP authentication and authorization to check subscriber identity and permission.

Some refusal responses can reveal private policy. When that matters, a notifier should return 200 and follow it with a NOTIFY whose contents could appear valid to the subscriber, so the response does not disclose whether access was granted.

SUBSCRIBE can create state and trigger one or more NOTIFY requests, creating denial-of-service and amplification risks. Implementations should require authentication with replay protection and should protect relevant headers and message bodies against modification. Implementations may encrypt sensitive state.
sections.plainLanguage: Notifiers should check who is subscribing because event state may be sensitive. Authentication, replay protection and careful error responses help prevent forged subscriptions and protect private information.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3265
sections.content:
RFC 6665 obsoletes RFC 3265 and incorporates changes based on implementation and interoperability experience. It removes implicit subscriptions except for the historical REFER behavior, deprecates dialog reuse, clarifies subscription timers and state handling, and adds a reason code for state that will not change.

The RFC also removes 202 as a distinct response for SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY: implementations treat an incoming 202 as 200 and must not generate 202 for those methods. It adds an IANA registry for termination reason codes and updates RFC 3261 and RFC 4660.
sections.plainLanguage: This revision clarifies how subscriptions, timers and notifications work. It also deprecates dialog reuse and adds a registry for reasons that subscriptions end.

items.label: Retry now
items.desc: The subscriber should create a new subscription.

items.label: Retry later
items.desc: The subscriber should wait before trying again.

items.label: Not authorized
items.desc: The subscriber should not try again.

items.label: Not refreshed
items.desc: The subscription expired without a refresh.

items.label: Authorization delayed
items.desc: The notifier could not obtain authorization in time.

items.label: Resource removed
items.desc: The monitored state no longer exists.

items.label: State will not change
items.desc: The subscriber should not subscribe again.
